name: Brain-Body Mass Allometry (Mammals)
source: Jerison (1973) Evolution of the Brain and Intelligence; Martin (1981) Nature 293:57; encephalization data compiled in Burger et al. (2019)
notes: Brain mass (g) vs body mass (kg) for diverse mammals. Exponent ~0.75. Data from multiple compilations.
justification: Multiplicative: brain mass scales with body mass via volumetric/metabolic constraints, a scale-free multiplicative process across orders of magnitude.

name: Lung Vital Capacity vs Body Mass (Mammals)
source: Stahl (1967) J Appl Physiol 22:453; Schmidt-Nielsen (1984) Scaling: Why is Animal Size so Important?
notes: Vital capacity (mL) vs body mass (kg). Published exponent ~1.03. Data for rat-to-human size range.
justification: Multiplicative: lung capacity is constrained by volumetric body geometry, yielding scale-free power-law allometry across body sizes.

name: Pareto Income Distribution (US Census 2020)
source: US Census Bureau (2020) Current Population Survey; Piketty & Saez (2003) QJE updated through 2020; Pareto (1896) Cours d'economie politique
notes: Number of tax units with income above threshold x (thousands). Upper tail follows Pareto power law with exponent ~1.5-2.
justification: Multiplicative: income is generated by multiplicative random shocks (Gibrat process), yielding power-law tails in wealth and income distributions.

name: Forest Fire Size Distribution (US Federal Lands)
source: Malamud et al. (1998) Science 281:1840; USFWS fire records 1986-1995
notes: Cumulative number of fires exceeding given area (acres). Power-law exponent ~1.3. Self-organised criticality.
justification: Multiplicative: fire spread is governed by multiplicative branching processes; each ignition multiplies fuel consumption, producing scale-free size distributions.

name: Stellar Initial Mass Function (Salpeter)
source: Salpeter (1955) ApJ 121:161; Kroupa (2001) MNRAS 322:231; Chabrier (2003) PASP 115:763
notes: Number of stars per unit mass interval dN/dM vs stellar mass (solar masses). Salpeter exponent alpha=2.35 for M>0.5 Msun.
justification: Multiplicative: gravitational fragmentation of molecular clouds follows multiplicative cascading, with each fragment mass determined by multiplicative splitting ratios.

name: River Discharge vs Drainage Area (US Streams)
source: Leopold & Maddock (1953) USGS Prof Paper 252; Vogel et al. (1999) JAWRA 35:1431
notes: Mean annual discharge (m3/s) vs drainage area (km2). Published exponent ~0.8. Eastern US rivers.
justification: Multiplicative: discharge accumulates via multiplicative aggregation of contributing sub-basins, each multiplying the flow by their drainage fraction.

name: Website Traffic vs Rank (Zipf/Alexa)
source: Adamic & Huberman (2002) Glottometrics 3:143; Alexa Internet (2014); Nielsen Norman Group
notes: Monthly unique visitors (millions) vs rank for top websites. Power-law exponent ~1.0.
justification: Multiplicative: web traffic follows preferential attachment (rich-get-richer), a multiplicative growth process producing power-law rank-size distributions.

name: City Road Network Length vs Population (Europe)
source: Bettencourt (2013) Science 340:1438; Molinero & Thurner (2021) J R Soc Interface 18:20200705
notes: Total road length (km) vs city population. Sub-linear exponent ~0.85. Data from European urban areas.
justification: Multiplicative: infrastructure scales as a fractal network embedded in 2D/3D space; road length is a power-law function of the spatial extent, which itself scales multiplicatively with population.

name: GDP per Capita vs Energy Use per Capita (Countries 2019)
source: World Bank (2019) World Development Indicators; IEA Energy Balances; Warr & Ayres (2010) Ecological Economics
notes: GDP per capita (2017 PPP $) vs primary energy use per capita (kWh). Cross-sectional data for 20 countries.
justification: Multiplicative: economic output scales with energy input via multiplicative production functions; each unit of energy is multiplied by productivity factors.

name: Benford's Law (First Digit Frequency)
source: Benford (1938) Proc Amer Philos Soc 78:551; Newcomb (1881) Am J Math 4:39; Hill (1995) Statistical Science 10:354
notes: Observed first-digit frequency from Benford's original 20,222 observations across 20 datasets. x is digit (1-9), y is observed percentage.
justification: Multiplicative: Benford's law emerges from multiplicative processes; data generated by successive multiplication yields logarithmically uniform distributions, producing the first-digit law.

name: Keeling Curve (Atmospheric CO2 Growth)
source: Keeling et al. (1976) Tellus 28:538; NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory; Scripps CO2 Program
notes: Annual mean atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa (ppm). Growth is approximately exponential over this period. Anthropogenic emissions add CO2 at rates proportional to economic growth.
justification: Additive: CO2 accumulates via additive annual emissions from fossil fuel combustion. The growth rate is additive (ppm/year increasing), not multiplicative.

name: Omori's Law (Northridge 1994 Aftershock Decay)
source: Shcherbakov et al. (2004) Geophys Res Lett 31:L11613; Utsu et al. (1995) J Phys Earth 43:1; USGS/SCSN catalog
notes: Aftershock rate (events/day, M>=2) vs days after Mw 6.7 Northridge mainshock. Modified Omori law: n(t) = K/(t+c)^p with p~1.1.
justification: Multiplicative: aftershock triggering is a multiplicative cascade; each aftershock can trigger further events with probability proportional to its magnitude, yielding power-law temporal decay.

name: World GDP Growth (Maddison Historical)
source: Maddison (2001) The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective, OECD; Bolt & van Zanden (2020) Maddison Project Database
notes: World GDP in billions of 1990 international Geary-Khamis dollars. Approximately exponential growth post-1800.
justification: Additive: GDP growth arises from additive increments to capital stock, labour, and productivity. Each year's growth adds to the existing base, creating exponential accumulation.

name: COVID-19 Antibody Waning (BNT162b2 IgG)
source: Levin et al. (2021) NEJM 385:e84; Israel et al. (2021) NEJM; Goldberg et al. (2021) NEJM
notes: Anti-spike IgG antibody levels (AU/mL) vs months after second BNT162b2 dose. Exponential decay with half-life ~50 days in first 6 months.
justification: Additive: antibody decay follows first-order kinetics, where a constant fraction is cleared per unit time (additive rate in log-space), yielding exponential decline.

name: Water Viscosity vs Temperature (NIST/IAPWS)
source: Korosi & Fabuss (1968) Anal Chem 40:157; Kestin et al. (1978) JPCRD 7:941; IAPWS-2008 Release on Viscosity
notes: Dynamic viscosity of water (mPa.s) vs temperature (C). Arrhenius-type exponential decrease. x expressed as 1000/T(K) for Arrhenius fit.
justification: Additive: viscosity follows Arrhenius form exp(Ea/RT), where temperature acts additively on the activation energy barrier in the exponent.

name: Radiocarbon Decay (C-14 in Tree Rings)
source: Libby (1955) Radiocarbon Dating; Godwin (1962) Nature 195:984; IntCal20 calibration curve
notes: Fraction of initial C-14 activity vs thousands of years before present. Half-life 5730 years.
justification: Additive: radioactive decay is a first-order process where constant fraction decays per unit time, yielding exponential decay in activity.

name: Beer-Lambert Optical Absorption
source: Beer (1852) Ann Phys 162:78; Swinehart (1962) J Chem Educ 39:333; Mayerhofer et al. (2016) ChemPhysChem 17:1948
notes: Transmitted light intensity (fraction) vs path length through 0.1M KMnO4 solution at 525 nm. Exponential decay I = I0 * 10^(-epsilon*c*l).
justification: Additive: each infinitesimal layer of absorbing medium removes a constant fraction of remaining intensity; path length acts additively in the exponent.

name: Capacitor Discharge (RC Circuit)
source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker (2013) Fundamentals of Physics; verified in Montazer & Bhattacharjee (2020) Am J Phys 88:1003
notes: Voltage (V) vs time (s) for discharging 1000 uF capacitor through 10 kohm resistor (RC = 10 s). Standard lab verification of exponential decay.
justification: Additive: charge leaks at a rate proportional to remaining voltage; time acts additively in the exponential. dV/dt = -V/RC.

name: World Population Growth (1800-2020)
source: UN Population Division (2022) World Population Prospects; Maddison (2001); US Census Bureau Historical Estimates
notes: World population (billions) follows logistic-like trajectory with inflection around 1987 and projected carrying capacity ~10-11 billion.
justification: Bounded: growth rate peaked in 1963 and has been declining; population is approaching a finite carrying capacity set by resource and demographic transition constraints.

name: US Television Adoption (Technology Diffusion)
source: US Census Bureau; Comin & Hobijn (2004) NBER WP 10886; Our World in Data Technology Adoption dataset
notes: Percentage of US households with television. Classic logistic S-curve diffusion.
justification: Bounded: adoption is bounded between 0% and 100% of households. Saturation is a hard ceiling.

name: US Internet Adoption (Technology Diffusion)
source: Pew Research Center Internet/Broadband Fact Sheet; ITU World Telecommunication Indicators; US Census Bureau CPS
notes: Percentage of US adults using the internet. Logistic S-curve with near-saturation by 2020.
justification: Bounded: internet adoption is bounded between 0% and 100% of the adult population. Infrastructure and demographic limits impose a ceiling.

name: Photosynthesis Light Response (Soybean)
source: Boote & Loomis (1991) in Modeling Crop Photosynthesis; Ye (2007) Ann Bot 99:955; USDA-ARS field data
notes: Net photosynthetic rate (umol CO2/m2/s) vs photosynthetically active radiation (umol photons/m2/s). Rectangular hyperbola (Michaelis-Menten-type) saturating response.
justification: Bounded: photosynthesis saturates because the number of photosynthetic reaction centres is finite. At high light, all centres are occupied and rate plateaus at Pmax.

name: Drug Dose-Response (Ibuprofen Analgesic Efficacy)
source: Laska et al. (1986) Clin Pharmacol Ther 40:1; McQuay & Moore (1998) An Evidence-Based Resource for Pain Relief; Cochrane Review (2009)
notes: Percentage of patients achieving at least 50% pain relief vs ibuprofen dose (mg). Sigmoidal dose-response with Hill coefficient ~2.
justification: Bounded: efficacy is bounded between 0% and maximum response (~100%). Receptor occupancy follows mass-action kinetics with finite receptor count.

name: Enzyme Kinetics: Lactate Dehydrogenase (Empirical)
source: Nakae & Stoward (1997) J Histochem Cytochem 45:1427; Bergmeyer (1974) Methods of Enzymatic Analysis
notes: Reaction velocity (umol/min/mg) vs L-lactate concentration (mM) for purified rabbit LDH-M4. Km ~22 mM.
justification: Bounded: enzyme velocity saturates at Vmax when all active sites are occupied. Michaelis-Menten kinetics with finite enzyme concentration.

name: Langmuir Adsorption Isotherm (N2 on Activated Carbon)
source: Brunauer et al. (1938) JACS 60:309; Rouquerol et al. (2014) Adsorption by Powders and Porous Solids, Elsevier
notes: Volume of N2 adsorbed (cm3 STP/g) vs relative pressure P/P0 at 77K. Type I isotherm = Langmuir monolayer saturation.
justification: Bounded: the surface has finite adsorption sites. Coverage approaches monolayer capacity asymptotically, bounded by total available sites.

name: Beverton-Holt Stock-Recruitment (North Sea Cod)
source: Beverton & Holt (1957) Fishery Investigations Series II Vol 19; ICES Stock Assessment Database; Myers et al. (1999) CJFAS 56:1400
notes: Recruitment (millions of age-1 fish) vs spawning stock biomass (thousand tonnes). Beverton-Holt: R = aS/(b+S).
justification: Bounded: recruitment saturates because density-dependent mortality (competition, predation) limits juvenile survival at high stock sizes. Carrying capacity imposes an asymptote.

name: Lithium-Ion Battery Capacity Fade (NMC Cycling)
source: Severson et al. (2019) Nature Energy 4:383; Attia et al. (2020) Nature 578:397; NREL battery degradation data
notes: Remaining capacity (% of initial) vs cycle number for NMC/graphite 18650 cells at 1C, 25C. Bounded decay towards end-of-life floor.
justification: Bounded: capacity is bounded between initial 100% and a floor set by irreversible side reactions (SEI growth). The degradation rate slows as active material loss saturates.

name: COVID-19 Cumulative Cases (Italy, Spring 2020)
source: Italian Civil Protection Department daily reports; WHO Situation Reports; Johns Hopkins CSSE COVID-19 Dashboard
notes: Cumulative confirmed COVID-19 cases in Italy during first wave (Feb-May 2020). Classic logistic/SIR epidemic curve.
justification: Bounded: cumulative cases are bounded by susceptible population size and intervention (lockdown). Herd immunity and NPIs impose a saturation ceiling.

name: Yeast Growth (Saccharomyces cerevisiae Logistic)
source: Carlson (1913) Biochem Z 57:313; Pearl (1927) QR Biol 2:532; Monod (1949) Ann Rev Microbiol 3:371
notes: Yeast population (millions/mL) vs time (hours) in batch culture. Classic logistic growth curve used by Pearl and Reed to validate logistic model.
justification: Bounded: yeast growth is limited by nutrient depletion and ethanol toxicity. Population approaches a carrying capacity set by medium composition.

name: Crop Yield Response to Nitrogen Fertiliser
source: Cerrato & Blackmer (1990) Agron J 82:138; Bullock & Bullock (1994) Agron J 86:191; Brentrup & Palliere (2010)
notes: Maize grain yield (tonnes/ha) vs nitrogen application rate (kg N/ha). Diminishing returns with saturation at ~12 t/ha.
justification: Bounded: yield is bounded by genetic potential, light, water, and other non-nitrogen resources. Once N is non-limiting, other constraints cap yield.

name: Predator Functional Response (Type II, Lynx-Hare)
source: Holling (1959) Canadian Entomologist 91:385; Dale et al. (1994) J Anim Ecol 63:925; O'Donoghue et al. (1998) Oikos 82:169
notes: Kill rate (hares/lynx/day) vs hare density (hares/km2). Type II functional response: saturating hyperbolic form analogous to Michaelis-Menten.
justification: Bounded: predator consumption rate is bounded by handling time; at high prey densities, all time is spent handling prey, imposing a maximum kill rate.

name: Monod Growth Kinetics (E. coli, Glucose-Limited)
source: Monod (1949) Ann Rev Microbiol 3:371; Shehata & Marr (1971) J Bacteriol 107:210; Kovacova et al. (2000)
notes: Specific growth rate (1/h) vs glucose concentration (mg/L) for E. coli in chemostat. Monod equation mu = mu_max * S/(Ks + S), Ks ~4 mg/L.
justification: Bounded: growth rate is bounded by maximum enzymatic processing speed (mu_max). At high substrate, all transport/enzyme sites are saturated.

name: Crater Diameter vs Impact Energy (Planetary)
source: Schmidt & Housen (1987) Int J Impact Engng 5:543; Holsapple (1993) Annu Rev Earth Planet Sci 21:333; Melosh (1989) Impact Cratering
notes: Crater diameter (km) vs impactor kinetic energy (joules). Power-law exponent ~0.29 (pi-scaling). Data from laboratory impacts and planetary craters.
justification: Multiplicative: crater formation is governed by point-source scaling laws where diameter depends on energy through dimensional analysis of gravitational and strength regimes -- a pure multiplicative power law.

name: Earthquake Energy vs Magnitude (Gutenberg-Richter Energy)
source: Gutenberg & Richter (1956) Ann Geofis 9:1; Kanamori (1977) JGR 82:2981; USGS Earthquake Hazards Program
notes: Seismic energy release (joules) vs magnitude. log10(E) = 1.5M + 4.8. Exponential in magnitude (which is itself a log measure).
justification: Additive: magnitude is a logarithmic measure; energy scales exponentially with magnitude because each unit increase adds a fixed increment to log(E), i.e. the operator is additive in log-space.

name: Newton's Law of Cooling (Coffee)
source: Walker (1977) The Flying Circus of Physics; verified in Vollmer (2009) Eur J Phys 30:S17; Arons & Peppard (1965) Am J Phys 33:442
notes: Temperature above ambient (delta-T, degrees C) vs time (minutes) for cooling coffee in ceramic mug. Ambient = 22C.
justification: Additive: heat loss rate is proportional to temperature difference (Newton). Time acts additively in the exponent: dT/dt = -k(T - T_ambient).

name: US Smartphone Adoption (Technology Diffusion)
source: Pew Research Center (2021) Mobile Fact Sheet; comScore MobiLens; Statista Digital Market Outlook
notes: Percentage of US adults owning a smartphone. Logistic S-curve approaching saturation ~96%.
justification: Bounded: smartphone ownership is bounded between 0% and ~100% of adult population. Market saturation imposes a hard ceiling.

name: Species Discovery Accumulation Curve (Birds of Colombia)
source: Soberron & Llorente (1993) Conservation Biology 7:480; Colwell & Coddington (1994) Phil Trans R Soc B 345:101; Chao & Jost (2012) Ann Rev Ecol Evol Syst 43:127
notes: Cumulative species discovered vs survey effort (collector-years). Saturating curve approaching total species richness asymptote.
justification: Bounded: the true species count is finite. As more surveys are conducted, the chance of finding a new species diminishes, producing saturating accumulation.

name: CPU Clock Speed Scaling (1970-2020)
source: Danowitz et al. (2012) IEEE Micro 32:89; Rupp (2020) 50 Years of Microprocessor Trend Data; Stanford CPU DB
notes: Maximum commercial CPU clock speed (GHz). Logistic saturation due to power wall and thermal limits around ~5 GHz.
justification: Bounded: clock frequency is bounded by power dissipation (P ~ f*V^2*C) and thermal limits. The 'power wall' imposed a hard ceiling around 2005.

name: Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve
source: Ebbinghaus (1885) Uber das Gedachtnis; Wixted & Ebbesen (1991) J Exp Psychol: Learn Mem Cogn 17:927; Rubin & Wenzel (1996) Psychol Bull 120:253
notes: Retention (% of learned nonsense syllables correctly recalled) vs time (hours). Power-law decay fits better than exponential. Wixted (1990) confirmed power-law superiority.
justification: Multiplicative: memory traces decay via a multiplicative interference process where each retrieval attempt and intervening learning multiplicatively reduces trace strength, producing power-law (not exponential) forgetting.

name: Earthquake Frequency-Magnitude (Japan, JMA Catalog)
source: Japan Meteorological Agency Seismic Catalog; Nanjo et al. (2004) JGR 109:B02302; Wiemer & Wyss (2000) BSSA 90:859
notes: Annual number of earthquakes >=M in Japan region. log10(N) = a - bM with b~1.0. Exponential decay in N vs M.
justification: Additive: magnitude is a logarithmic variable; in the Gutenberg-Richter relation, each unit increase in M additively decreases log10(N) by b, producing exponential decay of frequency with magnitude.
